name: Moose

surveys.narrative: Moose Lake contains average population of suckers, northern pike, walleyes, & smallmouth bass. Rock bass & tullibee are present in above average numbers while perch are some- what below average. The walleye population is made up of mostly younger fish. The 1977 year class appears to be quite poor, while the 1976, 1978, & 1979 year class look quite strong. Growth is about average for lakes in the Ely area, but low for the chain of lakes.

This assessment indicated above average population of northern pike and smallmouth bass; average populations of walleye, white sucker, and rock bass; and below average populations of perch and whitefish. Bluegills have never been taken in Moose Lake before (although it has been known they are present). The reason for the huge numbers taken here is unknown. The cisco population appears to be below other assessments although cisco show up well in newfound & sucker lakes. Walleye growth is excellent.

Northern pike and bluegill are present in above average numbers; white sucker, rock bass, smallmouth bass, yellow perch, and walleye are present in average numbers; cisco are present in below average numbers. Whitefish, captured in low numbers in previous assessments were absent in this assessment. Walleye and northern pike are larger than average; walleye growth is average until age III, then above average.

Northern pike and rock bass are present in above average numbers; Cisco, white sucker, smallmouth and largemouth bass, yellow perch, and walleye are present in average numbers; bluegill are present in below average numbers. Cisco sizes range from 7, recruitment of yellow perch and walleye appears fair. Walleye growth is average.

Fish populations are dominated by walleye and northern pike, followed by white sucker and cisco. Low numbers of rock bass, smallmouth bass, whitefish, and bluegill are also present. Cisco sizes range from 6 captured were small. Some (over 24 present. Walleye recruitment is erratic; most walleye are from stocked year classes. 1990 appeared to be a good year for walleye reproduction on the Moose Lake chain. Walleye growth is faster than average for the area.

Fish populations are dominated by white sucker, northern pike, and cisco, followed by walleye. Low populations of lake whitefish, rock bass, bluegill, smallmouth and largemouth bass, and yellow perch are also present. Smallmouth numbers are likely underestimated as many smallmouth catches are reported by anglers.Cisco sizes are small ranging from 6" to 13" and averaging 9.2". Some large (over 25") walleye are present.Reproduction of bluegill and northern pike is consistent. Walleye recruitment is variable; current walleye numbers are dominated by a strong 1990 year class.Growth of bluegill and northern pike is average for the area. Growth of younger walleye is average and then changes to above average (16.3" at Annulus IV in 1991 assessment).

Moose Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 7 but is smaller, deeper and has less littoral area, has clearer and more chemically fertile water, and has a rounder shoreline shape than most Class 7 lakes. It is part of a chain of large interconnected lakes, including Newfound, Sucker, and Birch Lakes, all to the northeast of Moose Lake. The total catch of fish (all species combined) in 1995 is similar to the long term average catch for this lake and is normal for this lake class. The total catch of fish in the trapnets in 1995 is higher than in previous trapnetting in 1972 and 1993, but the 1995 assessment was conducted earlier in the summer, when trapnet catches are usually higher. Fish populations in 1995 were dominated by northern pike, white sucker, walleye, and smallmouth bass. Northern pike numbers in 1995 were higher than the long term average for this lake and were also higher than normal for this lake class. Pike sizes averaged 21"; the largest pike captured was 35". Pike growth, 20" at age four, was good. Walleye numbers in 1995 were near the long term average for this lake, but were lower than normal for this lake class and lower than the other lakes in this system. Walleye sizes averaged 15"; the largest was 28". Walleye growth (16" at age four) was good.Smallmouth bass numbers in 1995 were higher than in most previous assessments in this lake and were also higher than normal for this lake class. Smallmouth sizes averaged 11"; the largest was 17". Most smallmouth were age four. Smallmouth growth (7" at age four) was slow. Rock bass numbers in 1995 were higher than normal for this lake class. Numbers of bluegill sunfish and yellow perch were normal.Many of the fish examined were infested with Neascus, also known as "black spot". A few bluegill, smallmouth, and walleye also had yellow grubs under the skin. Most cisco (tullibee) had grubs in their muscle. All these parasites are common to fish in this area; none can infect humans, and all are killed by cooking.Rusty crayfish (Orconectes rusticus) have been observed in adjacent Newfound, Sucker, and Birch lakes since 1989. Rusty crayfish were first observed in Moose Lake in 1995 - all in one gillnet in the east-central part of the lake. Rusty crayfish are native to the Ohio River Valley and were probably introduced to this area by anglers using them for bait.Another crayfish species, probably blue crayfish (Orconectes propinquus), was captured in Moose Lake in the 1993 and 1995 assessments. These crayfish were also present in Newfound and Birch Lakes during those years and were abundant in Basswood Lake (downstream of Sucker Lake) in a 1996 assessment. They are also an introduced species and are native in states to the south and east of Minnesota. Both rusty and blue crayfish have the potential to adversely affect fish populations in Moose Lake.

Moose Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 7, which consists of 41 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large, have very irregular shoreline shapes, and have very soft (unmineralized) water. Moose Lake is deeper, and has clearer and harder (more mineralized) water than most of the lakes in this lake class.Moose Lake was thermally stratified on 08/21/2000 and retained 2 ppm oxygen to a depth of 35 ft, where the temperature was 49 F. Moose Lake has six inlets, five of which originate in small nearby lakes; all of these inlets have barriers to fish movement. The outlet to Newfound Lake is 5 ft deep and is easily navigable by fish and boats. Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline are mostly boulder, rubble, gravel, and ledgerock. Aquatic plants are sparse and grow to a depth of 12 ft. Moose Lake ranks as mesotrophic according to Carlson's Trophic State Index and using a 4.0 m Secchi water clarity, 5.2 ppb Chlorophyll - a, and 33 ppb total phosphorus. There is a public access with a concrete ramp for motorboats and a canoe landing. There are 56 homes and cottages, and 10 resorts and outfitters with numerous motel units, bunkhouses, and campsites. The western half of Moose Lake is about 50 percent Federal land, 20 percent State land, and 30 percent private land. The eastern half of Moose Lake is in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness (BWCAW) which the United States Forest Service (USFS) administers. There are five campsites on the BWCAW portion of the lake maintained by the USFS. There are winter and summer use restrictions on the BWCAW portion of Moose Lake; quotas for motorboats and overnight campers, day use permits for day users, and a ban on snowmobiles in the winter. Moose Lake is the largest single entry point to the BWCAW. Fish sampling in this fisheries lake survey consisted of 12 gillnet sets, 12 trapnet sets, and 4 shoreline seine hauls. Previously, the initial fisheries lake survey (1972) and nine fish population assessments each consisted of 6-12 gillnet sets, most of which were done in August. Three of these investigations included 5-12 trapnet sets. Trapnetting in 1995 and 2000 was done in mid June.The total catch of fish (all species combined) in the gillnets in 2000 of 18.9 fish/net (31.9 lb/net) was in the second quartile for this lake class and was similar to the median catch of 24.5 fish/net (31.5 lb/net) in all investigations on this lake. Lake Class 7 is one of the most productive lake classes in northeast Minnesota, in terms of gillnet catches of fish.The total catch of fish in the trapnets in 2000 of 16.1 fish/net (7.6 lb/net) was higher than the median catch of 10.3 fish/net (5.8 lb/net) in all investigations on this lake. More bluegill were caught in 2000 (and in 1995) than in the earlier two trapnettings, perhaps due to the earlier trapnetting dates in 2000 and 1995. Fish populations in 2000 were dominated by northern pike, followed by smallmouth bass, white sucker, walleye, and bluegill sunfish. Other species were present in generally low numbers.Northern pike numbers in 2000 (5.0/gillnet) were in the fourth quartile for this lake class and were similar to the median catch of 4.3/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Pike sizes in 2000 averaged 23.6" (3.1 lb), which was in the third quartile for this lake class. The largest pike was 33.1". Pike scales were difficult to read, but growth was generally near the median for area lakes.Smallmouth bass numbers in 2000 in gillnets (0.3/gillnet) were in the normal range for this lake class while the trapnet catch (1.5/trapnet) was higher than normal for this lake class. Largemouth bass numbers in gillnets (0.2/gillnet) were near the first quartile for this lake class while the trapnet catch (1.1/trapnet) was in the fourth quartile for this lake class. These species are "net shy" and their numbers are often underrepresented in the gillnet and trapnet catches. Smallmouth are commonly caught by anglers on Moose Lake. The largest smallmouth in this investigation was 15.4" and the largest largemouth was 11.7". Growth of largemouth and smallmouth in 2000 were in the normal range for area lakes.White sucker numbers in 2000 (4.6/gillnet) were in the third quartile for this lake class and were similar to the median catch of 5.3/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Sucker sizes averaged 17.2"; the largest (caught in a trapnet) was 22.7".Walleye numbers in 2000 (3.0/gillnet) were at the first quartile for this lake class and were similar to the median catch of 3.3/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Walleye sizes in 2000 averaged 13.4" (1.2 lb), which was in the third quartile for this lake class. Walleye growth was near the median for area lakes.Bluegill were first observed in the 1983 assessment on Moose Lake. Bluegill numbers have increased and at 6.8/trapnet in 2000 were in the third quartile for this lake class. Bluegill sizes averaged 4.7"; the largest was 8.1". Bluegill growth was in the normal range for area lakes.Cisco numbers in 2000 (2.8/gillnet) were in the second quartile for this lake class and were lower than the median catch of 5.8/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Cisco sizes in 2000 averaged 9.3"; the largest was 13.3".Many of the walleye and northern pike examined in 2000 had neascus (black spot). Many of the cisco had trianophorus. All of the parasites found on fish during the 2000 survey on Moose Lake were common to the area. They cannot infect humans, are often removed by filleting, and are killed at temperatures used for cooking fish.Rusty crayfish were introduced into nearby Sucker Lake or Newfound Lake, probably by anglers using them for bait, and have been captured in the gillnets in Moose Lake in 1995 (0.8/gillnet) and in 2000 (1.4/gillnet).Blue crayfish, also probably introduced by anglers, were found in nearby Basswood Lake in 1996. Similar appearing crayfish were observed in Moose, Newfound, and Sucker lakes in 1993 and 1995 and were identified as "native" crayfish during those investigations. Blue crayfish (12.4/gillnet) were captured in the 2000 lake survey in Moose Lake.

Moose Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 7, which consists of 41 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large, have very irregular shoreline shapes, and have soft (unmineralized) water. Moose Lake is deeper and has clearer water than most of the lakes in this lake class. Moose Lake is a mesotrophic lake.Moose Lake was thermally stratified on 08/22/2005 with a surface temperature of 66 F and a bottom temperature of 48 F. Adequate oxygen for fish (more than 2 ppm) was retained to a depth of 50 ft, where the temperature was 48 F. Moose Lake has six small inlets, five of which originate in small nearby lakes. The outlet to Newfound Lake is 5 ft deep and easily navigable. Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline of Moose Lake are mostly boulder, rubble, gravel, and ledgerock. Aquatic plants are sparse and grow to a depth of 12 ft.There is a public access with a concrete boat ramp and a canoe landing. There are about 60 homes and cottages, and about 10 resorts, canoe outfitters, and camps, with numerous motel units, bunkhouses, and campsites. All of the private development, which comprises about 30 percent of the shoreline, is on the southwestern shore of the lake. The northeastern half of Moose Lake is in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness (BWCAW), which is administered by the US Forest Service. Moose Lake is the largest single entry point to the BWCAW and has five water-access campsites. There are winter and summer use restrictions on the BWCAW portion of Moose Lake: quotas and permits for motorboats and overnight campers, day use permits for day visitors, 25 horsepower maximum motor size for motorboats, and a ban on snowmobile use in the winter. Fish sampling in the 2005 fish population assessment consisted of 12 gillnet sets and 12 trapnet sets. Eleven previous fisheries investigations dating back to 1972 each used 6-12 gillnets. Four of these previous investigations used 5-12 trapnets. Shoreline seining to evaluate natural reproduction was done in the 2000 investigation. Shoreline seining and small mesh trapnetting was done in 1967-68 and in 1971-72 in an effort to evaluate walleye fry stocking.Fish populations in 2005, as in most previous investigations, were dominated by walleye, northern pike, white sucker, and cisco. Also captured in 2005 were high numbers of bluegill sunfish. Walleye numbers in 2005 (4.8/gillnet) were in the second quartile for this lake class and were similar to the median walleye catch of 4.1/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Walleye sizes in 2005 averaged 16.4" (2.0 lb), which was in the fourth quartile for this lake class and was larger than the average size of 15.0" in all investigations on this lake. The largest walleye was 30.6". Most walleye captured in 2005 were ages 2-4. Walleye growth was somewhat faster than normal (in the third quartile) by area standards.Northern pike numbers in 2005 (7.3/gillnet) were in the fourth quartile for this lake class and were higher than the median pike catch of 4.4/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Pike sizes in 2005 averaged 21.6" (2.4 lb), which was in the second quartile for this lake class and was smaller than the average size of 23.3" in all investigations on this lake. The largest pike was 38.5". Most pike captured in 2005 were ages 3-5. Pike growth was somewhat slower than normal by area standards (in the second quartile).Cisco and sucker numbers in 2005 were lower than normal for this lake class and lower than the long term medians for this lake. Cisco sizes in 2005 ranged from 6" to 14".Bluegill were first captured in shoreline seines in 1968-72, but were not captured in standard trapnets in the first fisheries lake survey in 1972. Their numbers in subsequent investigations increased from 1.2/trapnet in 1993 to 4.4/trapnet in 1995, 6.8/trapnet in 2000, and to 29.2/trapnet in 2005. The trapnetting dates were standardized in 1995 to mid-June, so the recent increase in bluegill numbers appears to be real and not due to changes in sampling dates. Increases in bluegill numbers have been observed in a number of area lakes in recent years, perhaps due to favorable conditions caused by longer and warmer summers. Bluegill sizes in 2005 averaged 6.1"; the largest (caught in a gillnet) was 8.4". Bluegill recruitment was erratic, with most bluegill in the 2005 trapnet catch being age four or seven. Bluegill growth was somewhat slower than normal by area standards (in the second quartile).Non-native crayfish were first observed in Moose Lake in the 1991 investigation, when they were caught entangled in gillnets. Typical of recent crayfish catches in Moose Lake, the 2005 catch consisted of a native species (Orconectes virilis - 0.2/gillnet), and two non-native species: O. propinquus (5.8/gillnet) and O. rusticus (8.5/gillnet). These numbers are relatively low; abundant populations of rusty crayfish (more than 100/gillnet) have decimated aquatic vegetation in some area lakes and have been implicated in the decline of sunfish populations. These non-native species are also found in Newfound, Sucker, Birch, and Basswood lakes.Neascus (black spot) was found on many of the game fish examined in 2005. Bass tapeworm was found in most of the smallmouth bass examined internally. Yellow grub was found on one of the yellow perch. All of these parasites are native to the area and are common. They cannot infect humans, are often removed by filleting fish, and are killed at temperatures used to cook fish.

Moose Lake is located approximately 17 miles NE of Ely, MN. It has a surface area of 1,211 acres and a maximum depth of 65 feet. Moose Lake was thermally stratified on 08/23/2010, the first day of the survey, with a surface temperature of 70* F and a bottom temperature of 50* F. Water clarity is above average compared to lakes in this class. There is a public access with two concrete boat ramps and a separate carry-down canoe landing. The NE half of the lake is within the BWCAW. Moose Lake is the largest entry point to the BWCAW. Walleye numbers in 2010 (4.4/gill net) were identical to the long term average for all assessments on this lake. Walleye sizes in 2010 averaged 16.7" and the growth rate was faster than average compared to lakes in this class. The largest walleye observed was 25". Northern pike numbers in 2010 (5.7/gill net) were higher than the long term average of 4.5/gill net for all assessments on this lake. Pike sizes in 2010 averaged 22.1" and the growth rate was slower than average compared to lakes in this class. The largest northern pike observed was 37". Bluegill numbers in 2010 (11.4/trap net) were higher than the long term average of 6.8/trap net for all assessments on this lake. Bluegill sizes in 2010 averaged 6.5" and the growth rate was slower than average compared to lakes in this class. The largest bluegill observed was 8". Smallmouth and largemouth bass were sampled in 2010. Their numbers are likely underestimated since they are net shy. Other game fish sampled were rock bass, pumpkinseed sunfish and yellow perch. Lake whitefish are also present. Two species of non-native crayfish were sampled in 2010. Rusty crayfish(25.1/gill net) were more abundant than Clearwater crayfish (1.5/gill net).

Moose Lake is located approximately 17 miles northeast of Ely. Approximately 50% of the lake lies within the BWCAW where a 25 hp maximum motor exists. Other BWCAW regulations apply and visitors should be familiar with them. Moose Lake is one of three connected lakes often referred to locally as the Moose Lake Chain. There is a double concrete ramp with a center dock located near the southeast shore of the lake off the Moose Lake Road for public access. Another carry-down access is nearby for visitors using canoes. There are several designated US Forest Service campsites on the lake for overnight use. Moose Lake is the most heavily used entry point in the BWCAW with visitors often heading towards Basswood Lake and points beyond. Walleye (29%) and northern pike (28%) were the most common gamefish species sampled during the 2018 survey on Moose Lake. White sucker (29%) were also common in the catch. Other species sampled in 2018 include bluegill, largemouth bass, rock bass, smallmouth bass and yellow perch. Walleye numbers in 2018 (5.4/gill net) were above the historic average (4.4/gill net) for this lake and below average (6.2/gill net) when compared to other area lakes that are similar. The average walleye sampled was 15.9 inches long and about 4 years old. Approximately 72% of the walleye sampled were 12 inches or larger. The largest walleye sampled in 2018 measured 27.4 inches. Northern pike numbers in 2018 (5.3/gill net) were above the historic average (4.5/gill net) for this lake and above average (2.1/gill net) compared to other similar area lakes. The average pike sampled was 24.2 inches long. Approximately 34% of the pike sampled in 2018 were 24 inches or larger with a maximum length of 37.1 inches recorded.

Moose Lake is a 1,301-acre lake located approximately 15 miles northeast of Ely. Most boaters and canoeists reach the lake through one of two ways. The U.S. Forest Service maintains a public access, on the East shore, that has a double concrete boat ramp and canoe landing area with ample parking. Other boaters and canoeists go through private shoreline on the Southwest corner of the lake, including several canoe outfitters, seasonal cabins, and permanent residences. The lake is in the Superior National Forest, and although roughly 60% of the lake is located within the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness (BWCAW), outboard motors up to 25 hp are allowed. The U.S. Forest Service maintains five campsites and visitors must have appropriate permits, issues by the U.S. Forest Service, to visit this portion of the lake. The southwest portion of the lake has no campsites or motor restrictions. The lake has a maximum depth of 65 feet and moderately clear water that is subject to algae blooms later in the summer. Moose Lake was thermally stratified on August 5, 2024. Water temperatures were 74 F at the surface and dropped to 49 F near the bottom, with adequate oxygen levels for species in the lake to a depth of about 40 feet. There are numerous small inlets around the lake, with all water flowing northeast to the other two lakes, Newfound and Sucker, that combine with Moose to make up the Moose Lake Chain. The Moose Lake Chain flows into Basswood Lake at Prairie Portage, and this connection is a primary reason that Moose Lake is one of the most used BWCAW entry points. Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline are mostly ledge rock, rubble, and gravel. Aquatic plants are rare, except for a few shallow bays where vegetation is concentrated. The overall gillnet catch rate was 21.2 fish/net which was slightly below average compared to past catches for the lake. Fish species sampled in gillnets included walleye, white sucker, rock bass, smallmouth bass, northern pike, black crappie, bluegill, burbot, and yellow perch. The overall trap net catch rate was 10.3 fish/net, which was also slightly below average for the lake. Species sampled in trap nets included bluegill, black crappie, largemouth bass, rock bass, yellow perch, northern pike, smallmouth bass, walleye, and white sucker. Walleye numbers in 2024 (10.7 fish/gillnet) were the highest ever recorded for a survey on Moose Lake and ranked above average for lakes within the Tower area. Lengths ranged from 8 to over 28 inches with an average of 16 inches, which was slightly larger than previous surveys. Growth was fast compared to other lakes in the area, as it took less than 4 years for the average walleye to reach 15 inches. Ages ranged from 2 to 12 years. Recruitment was remarkably consistent for this naturally reproducing population. Northern pike numbers in 2024 (1.3 fish/gillnet) were below average for the lake. Lengths ranged from 18 to 27 inches with an average of 22 inches, which was slightly smaller than previous surveys. Although not present in this survey, Moose Lake has a history of producing large pike, with the largest fish in a survey measuring 42 inches. Smallmouth bass numbers in 2024 (1.6 fish/gillnet) were the highest of any survey on Moose Lake. Lengths ranged from 7 to over 19 inches, which was the largest smallmouth ever sampled from the lake. Smallmouth averaged about 12 inches in length, which is slightly larger than previous surveys. Bluegill numbers in 2024 (7.2 fish/trap net) were above average for the lake. Lengths ranged from 4 to 8 inches with an average of about 6 inches, which was about average for the lake. Bluegill grew relatively fast compared to other area lakes, with the average fish reaching 6 inches in 4 to 5 years. Rusty crayfish are a non-native invasive species that were first documented in the Moose Chain in 1989. They were likely introduced in anglers' bait buckets. In 2024, the rusty crayfish catch rate was 64 crayfish/gillnet. This catch rate was similar compared to past surveys.

Temperature and dissolved oxygen measurements were collected from the deepest basin in Moose Lake on August 7th, 2025. This was done to evaluate the quantity and quality of cold, oxygenated water (i.e., oxythermal habitat) available to Lake Whitefish, the most sensitive coldwater species present in this lake (Cisco, also known as 'Tullibee', are also present). Lake Whitefish require a layer of oxythermal habitat that contains water temperatures below 17.2 degrees C (63.0 degrees F) and dissolved oxygen concentrations above 3.0 mg/L. Based on data collected from the deepest basin (maximum sampled depth was 64.9 feet), the water temperature decreased to 17.2 degrees C (63.0 degrees F) at 21.2 feet and the dissolved oxygen concentration decreased to 3.0 mg/L at 38.0 feet at the time of sampling. This layer in the water column was 16.9 feet, indicating oxythermal habitat for Lake Whitefish was present. Further, the temperature at which dissolved oxygen decreased to 3.0 mg/L (i.e., TDO3, a single variable to characterize oxythermal habitat) was 8.7 degrees C (47.7 degrees F). TDO3 values cooler than 17.2 degrees C (63.0 degrees F) indicate that oxythermal conditions were suitable for Lake Whitefish at the time of the survey. Data collected by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources during the period of maximum oxythermal stress (July 26th to Aug 24th) in 2010, 2018, 2024 also indicated suitable oxythermal habitat in all years surveyed, with the least favorable conditions recorded in 2010 when the suitable oxythermal habitat layer was 1.6 feet thick. When adequate oxythermal habitat is not available, Lake Whitefish are squeezed into unfavorable, warmer water conditions and experience higher levels of stress. In fisheries surveys since 1972, Lake Whitefish catches have been minimal or absent in 15 surveys.
